tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

## X2

### Explanations of what no one can hear: how much of an audio model's decision, and of its explanation, lies below the masking threshold

Every bin of a spectrogram is either audible or masked by louder neighbours, and the masking threshold from psychoacoustics (the model inside MP3) says which. Deleting all energy below the threshold is a change no listener can hear. You will build the threshold, delete the sub-threshold energy, and measure per model how much of the decision and how much of the attribution mass disappears, across five tasks and three architectures. Then you will test whether that number predicts a model's accuracy drop under codecs, which discard the same energy first, and audit listenable explanations for the share of their audio that nobody can hear.

measurement
course form: own experiment, with a new metric and a software package
compute: one workstation GPU

#### The question

How much of what audio models compute rests on inaudible energy, how much of their explanations points at it, and does inaudible reliance predict a model's robustness to codecs?

#### What is known

Psychoacoustic attacks on speech recognition (2018, 2019) hide perturbations under the masking threshold and succeed, which shows that models respond to energy listeners cannot hear. A 2026 causal analysis finds that a practically inaudible change to one frequency flips an audio classifier's decision in over half the cases. Codec robustness of deepfake detectors (2025) and of provenance attribution (2026) was measured without its cause. Listenable explanations (2022, 2024) return audio the user is meant to hear, with no check that it is audible. A 2026 preprint moves the attribution maps of deepfake detectors with inaudible perturbations. Nobody has measured inaudible reliance as a property of models and of explanations, or linked it to codec robustness.

#### Terms used

masking threshold
: the level, per time-frequency bin, below which a listener cannot hear energy because louder neighbouring sound masks it. Computed by a psychoacoustic model from the signal itself.

sub-threshold deletion
: removing every bin below the threshold and resynthesizing the waveform. By construction the listener hears no change.

inaudible reliance
: the change in a model's output under sub-threshold deletion, and the share of an attribution map's mass in sub-threshold bins.

#### First steps

- Implement the masking threshold (the MPEG psychoacoustic model, or an open implementation you have checked) and confirm on ten clips, by listening, that the sub-threshold deletion is inaudible to the team.
- Run one classifier on 100 clips before and after the deletion and report the output change against the change between two different clips.
- Write down the refuting result.

#### Plan

- Set up five tasks with public models and data: speech recognition (Whisper), speaker verification, sound tagging (the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs), bird sound classification (BirdNET), and deepfake detection (AASIST, a SONICS detector). Use three architectures where the task has them and 300 clips per task.
- Measure the decision change under sub-threshold deletion per model and task, with the between-clip control and bootstrap intervals, at two stated playback levels and with two masking models.
- Measure the inaudible mass of four attribution methods (Integrated Gradients, Grad-CAM, LRP, occlusion) on the common grid, with a random-map control.
- Measure each model's accuracy drop under MP3 and Opus at three bitrates and test whether inaudible reliance predicts it across models.
- Audit listenable maps: the share of a listenable explanation's energy below the threshold of the mix it is played in. Build an audible-by-construction variant (masks restricted to audible bins) and report its faithfulness cost.
- Release the threshold code, the deletion, the metric and the tables as a package.

#### What you deliver

You deliver an inaudible-reliance number for about fifteen model-and-task pairs and an inaudible-mass number for every explainer on them, the codec-prediction table, the audibility audit of listenable maps with the audible variant, and a package that computes the metric on any model. If the numbers are near zero everywhere, you have shown that these models hear what listeners hear, and the metric becomes a certificate worth reporting.

#### What would refute it

The decision change and the attribution mass below threshold stay within the between-clip control for every model and task, at both playback levels and under both masking models.

#### Where the paper could go

Interspeech. ICASSP. WASPAA. A machine learning venue if the codec prediction holds.

#### What you need

Whisper, a speaker verifier, the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs, BirdNET, AASIST, a SONICS detector. LibriSpeech, a VoxCeleb test set, ESC-50 or an AudioSet evaluation subset, a bird sound set, ASVspoof 2019, SONICS. An MP3 and Opus encoder. Captum, Zennit. The listenable-maps code. One GPU, inference only.

#### Compute

one workstation GPU

#### Watch out for

A masking model is an approximation and depends on the playback level. State the level, use two masking models and report both. Resynthesis after deletion can add artifacts of its own. Check the deletion by ear on a sample of every task and keep the phase. The bird sound set's licence must allow research use.

#### Read first

- Adversarial Attacks Against Automatic Speech Recognition Systems via Psychoacoustic Hiding ([arXiv:1808.05665](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05665))
- Imperceptible, Robust, and Targeted Adversarial Examples for Automatic Speech Recognition ([arXiv:1903.10346](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10346))
- I Guess That's Why They Call it the Blues: Causal Analysis for Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2601.16675](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16675))
- Measuring the Robustness of Audio Deepfake Detection under Real-World Corruptions ([arXiv:2503.17577](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17577))
- Clean Accuracy Does Not Guarantee Provenance Robustness: A Prospective Codec-Stress Evaluation of Audio Attribution ([arXiv:2609.07981](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07981))
- Listen to Interpret: Post-hoc Interpretability for Audio Networks with NMF ([arXiv:2202.11479](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11479))
- Listenable Maps for Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2403.13086](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13086))
- Listenable Maps for Zero-Shot Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2405.17615](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17615))
- The Perceived Fragility of Explanations in Audio Models: Manipulation of Attribution with Unchanged Predictions ([arXiv:2606.14466](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14466))
- A Framework for Evaluating Faithfulness in Explainable AI for Machine Anomalous Sound Detection ([arXiv:2601.19017](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19017))

## Toolbox

You can use any tools you like. Say in the paper what you used. Good starting points: Captum and Zennit for attribution, Quantus for metrics, the audioLIME repository for LIME on audio. Compare maps on one common time-frequency grid so that numbers across models mean the same thing. Give every claim a control (a random map, or a random perturbation of the same size) and report bootstrap intervals over clips. Call a difference a difference only when the intervals say so.

Datasets you can start from: ASVspoof 2019 and 2021, In-the-Wild, PartialSpoof, SONICS, FakeMusicCaps, LibriSpeech, a VoxCeleb test set, ESC-50, a bird sound set, a public MIDI corpus. Models you can start from: AASIST, RawNet2, a wav2vec 2.0 detector, the SONICS detectors, the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs, Whisper, BirdNET, the listenable-maps code. Check every licence before you download.
# SIWY
# Experiments on Kaggle

This document describes a method to run experiments with models on Kaggle from a local repository. It is a collection of rules and lessons from real projects. A project can use only the parts that it needs, and change them for its own work.

The local machine has the code and the records. Kaggle does the heavy computation. Git connects the two.

## 1. Local setup

The local machine needs these items:

| Item | Where | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Kaggle account | kaggle.com | Do the phone verification (Settings). Without it, a kernel gets no GPU and no internet. |
| Python environment | `.venv` in the root folder of the repository | Make it with uv (see the README or the instructions of the repository). |
| Kaggle CLI | the package `kaggle` in `requirements.txt` | Install it into `.venv`. Version 2.2.5 works. Call it only through `jobs/kaggle.sh`. |
| API token | `~/.kaggle/access_token` or `.kaggle/access_token` of the project | On kaggle.com, open Settings, API, and generate a new token. Write the token into the file as one line. |
| Access to the data | the private Kaggle dataset of the project | The owner of the dataset shares it with the account. |
| Git remote | a public repository with the project branch | The kernels clone the code from it (section 4). |

Do these steps:

1. Install the environment:

   ```bash
   uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
   uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt
   ```

2. Write the token into a file (see "Select the Kaggle account").
3. Do a test of the connection. The command shows the kernels of the account:

   ```bash
   bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels list --mine
   ```

Do not commit the token. It gives full access to the account.

### Select the Kaggle account

The script `jobs/kaggle.sh` selects the token. Then it runs the Kaggle CLI from `.venv`. People, agents and other scripts use the same command. Nobody sets an environment variable or gives the token in a command.

| Token file | Account |
|---|---|
| `.kaggle/access_token` in the project folder, not empty | The account of the project. Only this project uses it. |
| No project token | The personal account of the machine (`~/.kaggle/access_token`). All projects without a project token use it. |

The project token has priority. The script gives it to the CLI in the variable `KAGGLE_API_TOKEN`.

To use the personal account, do these steps once on each machine:

1. Write the token into the file:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/.kaggle
   echo "<token>" > ~/.kaggle/access_token
   chmod 600 ~/.kaggle/access_token
   ```

2. Make sure that the project has no `.kaggle/access_token`, or that the file is empty.

To use a different account for one project, do these steps in the project folder:

1. Make sure that `.gitignore` has the line `.kaggle/`.
2. Write the token of the project account into the file:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p .kaggle
   echo "<token>" > .kaggle/access_token
   chmod 600 .kaggle/access_token
   ```

3. Check the account. The line `username` must show the project account:

   ```bash
   bash jobs/kaggle.sh config view
   ```

`.gitignore` prevents an accidental commit of the token. It does not hide the token from a program of the same user.

### `jobs/kaggle.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run the Kaggle CLI of the project with the correct account.
# Usage: bash jobs/kaggle.sh <arguments of the kaggle command>
# If .kaggle/access_token of the project is not empty, the CLI uses this token.
# Otherwise the CLI uses the personal credentials (~/.kaggle/access_token).
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
TOKEN="$ROOT/.kaggle/access_token"
# The value, not the path: a Windows Python does not know the Git Bash paths.
if [ -s "$TOKEN" ]; then
  export KAGGLE_API_TOKEN="$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$TOKEN")"
fi
for KAGGLE in "$ROOT/.venv/Scripts/kaggle.exe" "$ROOT/.venv/bin/kaggle"; do
  [ -x "$KAGGLE" ] && exec "$KAGGLE" "$@"
done
echo "kaggle.sh: no Kaggle CLI in $ROOT/.venv" >&2
exit 127
```

The script looks for `.kaggle/` and `.venv/` in the folder above `jobs/`. Change `ROOT` for a different structure. The examples in this document call the script from the project folder.

## 2. Platform facts

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| GPU machine | `"machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4"` gives 2x Tesla T4, 15 GB of memory each. |
| GPU sessions at the same time | 2 for each account. A third push fails with "Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached". |
| GPU time | A weekly quota (approximately 30 hours). A session counts its hours, not the number of its GPUs. |
| CPU sessions | 4 cores and approximately 30 GB of RAM. They do not use the GPU quota. |
| Session limit | 12 hours. |
| Output folder | `/kaggle/working/`, approximately 20 GB. Only this folder is kept after the session. |
| Temporary folder | `/kaggle/temp/`. It is deleted after the session. |
| Input data | `/kaggle/input/<slug>/...`, read-only. |
| Python | 3.13 (2026). The local environment can differ. Do not use features of one version only. |
| Account | GPU and internet need a phone verification of the account. Without it, a GPU kernel runs on the CPU and no error occurs. |

Important behavior:

- If a kernel fails (status ERROR), Kaggle deletes its complete output. Hours of results can be lost.
- The CLI cannot stop a kernel. Only the web page can cancel it.
- The CLI does not give the version ID of a run. Thus use one kernel (notebook) for each job, not many versions of one kernel.
- `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels logs -f <user>/<project>-<job name>` shows the live log. The output of child processes is sometimes not in it.
- Use `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels status <user>/<project>-<job name>` for the state: QUEUED, RUNNING, COMPLETE, ERROR or CANCEL.

## 3. Repository structure

```
<project>/
  src/                    all logic (Python modules)
  jobs/
    JOBS.md               the list of all jobs and their status
    kaggle.sh             runs the Kaggle CLI with the token of the project or the personal token
    wait.sh               follows one kernel and writes its status into JOBS.md
    runs/
      YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job>/  one folder for each job (NN: the number of the job in the project)
        run.py              the script that Kaggle runs
        kernel-metadata.json
        <codename>.yaml     one config for each experiment of the job
        output/             the small results, with the same paths as /kaggle/working/
          <codename>/       metrics.json, report_*.csv, train_log.csv, ...
```

### Names

The job folder `YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>` identifies a job. NN is the number of the job in the project (01, 02, 03, ...). It does not start again on a new day. Thus the folders sort in the order of the jobs, and the number alone identifies a job. One job folder is one Kaggle kernel and one row in `JOBS.md`.

| Name | Where it occurs |
|---|---|
| Job folder, for example `2026-11-01_16_unet-v7ab` | The folder in `jobs/runs/` and the column Folder in `JOBS.md`. |
| Job name: the last part of the job folder, for example `unet-v7ab` | The kernel id (`<user>/<project>-unet-v7ab`), the column Job in `JOBS.md`, the second argument of `wait.sh`. |
| Codename, for example `unet-v7a` | The config file (`unet-v7a.yaml`), the output folder (`output/unet-v7a/`), and a table of results, if the project has one. |

- Each name is unique in the project. A search for a name finds all files of this job or experiment.
- A job has one or more codenames: one config file and one output folder for each codename.
- Variants of one idea get letters: `unet-v7a`, `unet-v7b`, `unet-v7c`, `unet-v7d`.
- The job name is the common part of its codenames plus their letters. The job `unet-v7ab` runs `unet-v7a` and `unet-v7b`, and the job `unet-v7cd` runs `unet-v7c` and `unet-v7d`.
- If a job has only one experiment, its codename is the job name.
- Use only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Kaggle makes the kernel slug from the title, and other characters change.

### Rules

- A job is one Kaggle kernel. A job can run more than one experiment (codename), for example one on each GPU.
- The config of an experiment is in the folder of the job that runs it. There is no separate folder for configs.
- The folder of a job does not change after the start. A new variant gets a new folder.
- The job folders are in `jobs/runs/`. Thus `jobs/` shows only `JOBS.md`, `kaggle.sh`, `wait.sh` and `runs/`, also when there are many jobs.
- `output/` keeps only small files. Data, model weights and caches stay on Kaggle.

A function finds a config from its codename:

```python
RUNS_DIR = PROJECT_DIR / "jobs" / "runs"

def load_config(codename: str) -> dict:
    matches = sorted(RUNS_DIR.glob(f"*/{codename}.yaml"))
    if len(matches) != 1:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"need exactly one config for {codename}, found {matches}")
    cfg = yaml.safe_load(matches[0].read_text())
    cfg["codename"] = codename
    return cfg
```

Lines for `.gitignore`. They keep data, model weights and logs out of git:

```
**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.npy
**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.npz
**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.log
*.pt
*.zip
```

## 4. Code and data on Kaggle

### Code

The kernel clones the project branch from a public repository. Thus every run uses code from git, and the commit hash goes into the log. Push the code before the push of the kernel.

If the repository has more than one project, clone only the project folder with a sparse checkout. The templates below do this. If the project is the complete repository, clone the complete repository and remove the `sparse-checkout` line:

```python
subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, REPO, CLONE], check=True)
sys.path.insert(0, CLONE)
```

Clone into `/tmp`, not into `/kaggle/working`. Otherwise the clone becomes a part of the output.

### Data

- Keep the data in a private Kaggle dataset. Upload the original zip as one file, not thousands of small files. Share the dataset with the team.
- The output of one kernel can be the input of another kernel: `"kernel_sources": ["<user>/<project>-<job name>"]`. Thus a data set or model weights from one job go to the next job without a download.
- The path under `/kaggle/input` can change. Find files with a recursive search, for example `Path("/kaggle/input").rglob("val.npy")`.
- To make a dataset from a kernel output, use the page of the kernel: Output, New Dataset. Kaggle extracts a zip to a folder with the name of the zip. If the output also has a folder with this name, the creation fails ("Directory already exists"). Thus give a zip a name like `<codename>-set.zip`.

### `kernel-metadata.json`

```json
{
  "id": "<user>/<project>-<job name>",
  "title": "<project>-<job name>",
  "code_file": "run.py",
  "language": "python",
  "kernel_type": "script",
  "is_private": true,
  "enable_gpu": true,
  "enable_internet": true,
  "machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4",
  "dataset_sources": ["<user>/<dataset>"],
  "competition_sources": [],
  "kernel_sources": []
}
```

For a CPU job, use `"enable_gpu": false` and remove `machine_shape`.

The `<user>` in the `id` must be the username of the account that `jobs/kaggle.sh` selects. Otherwise the push and the status fail with "Permission denied".

### `run.py` for one experiment on one GPU

```python
"""<What the job does, in one or two sentences.>"""
import subprocess
import sys

REPO = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>.git"
BRANCH = "<project branch>"
PROJECT = "<project folder>"
CLONE = "/tmp/repo"  # Not in the output folder, so the clone is not an output.
CODENAMES = ["<codename>"]

import torch

# A long job on the CPU wastes hours, so stop immediately without a GPU.
assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "no GPU: check the phone verification of the account"

subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse", REPO, CLONE], check=True)
subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "sparse-checkout", "set", PROJECT], check=True)
print("commit", subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "rev-parse", "HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
sys.path.insert(0, f"{CLONE}/{PROJECT}")

from src.config import load_config
from src.experiment import run_experiment

for codename in CODENAMES:
    run_experiment(load_config(codename))
```

## 5. Use of the two GPUs

A T4 x2 session has two GPUs, and the quota counts the session. A job that uses one GPU wastes half of its cost.

One process on each GPU uses both GPUs. Each process does its own work: one experiment, or one half of the data (shard).

### `run.py` for two experiments, one on each GPU

```python
"""Run two experiments at the same time, one on each GPU."""
import subprocess
import sys

REPO = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>.git"
BRANCH = "<project branch>"
PROJECT = "<project folder>"
CLONE = "/tmp/repo"  # Not in the output folder, so the clone is not an output.
CODENAMES = ["<codename a>", "<codename b>"]


def run(codename: str, gpu: int) -> None:
    sys.path.insert(0, f"{CLONE}/{PROJECT}")
    from src.config import load_config
    from src.experiment import run_experiment
    run_experiment(load_config(codename), f"cuda:{gpu}")


# A new process imports this file again, so the clone and the start must be only in the main process.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import torch

    assert torch.cuda.device_count() == 2, "this job needs 2 GPUs (T4 x2)"
    subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse", REPO, CLONE], check=True)
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "sparse-checkout", "set", PROJECT], check=True)
    print("commit", subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "rev-parse", "HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
    with torch.multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Pool(2) as pool:
        pool.starmap(run, [(codename, gpu) for gpu, codename in enumerate(CODENAMES)])
```

Rules for this pattern:

- Use the `spawn` context. CUDA does not work in a process from `fork`.
- Put the main code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`. Each new process imports `run.py` again.
- The experiment function gets the device as an argument, and it calls `torch.cuda.set_device(device)`.
- Each process writes its results into its own folder, `/kaggle/working/<codename>/`.
- The main process must not keep GPU memory. If it used the GPU before the start of the pool, call `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`. In one job, the main process kept 12 GB of cache on GPU 0, and the process for GPU 0 failed with "CUDA out of memory".
- If one process fails, the complete job fails, and Kaggle deletes the output of both experiments. Thus do a smoke test first (section 7).
- Two jobs with two experiments each give four experiments at the same time.
- Two processes share the RAM of the session. Each process must stay below approximately half of it.

For a CPU job, use `multiprocessing.Pool(4)` for the 4 cores.

## 6. Start and follow a job

### Start

1. Commit and push the code.
2. Add a row to `jobs/JOBS.md` with the status `to run`.
3. Push the kernel and start `wait.sh` for it.

The push sends `run.py` and `kernel-metadata.json` of the job folder to Kaggle and starts the kernel:

```bash
# From the project folder:
bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels push -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>
```

Output if the push is correct:

```
Kernel version 1 successfully pushed.  Please check progress at https://www.kaggle.com/code/<user>/<project>-<job name>
```

The first push makes the kernel. A second push of the same folder makes version 2 of the same kernel.

If two GPU sessions are active, the push fails. This loop tries again until a slot is free, and then follows the job:

```bash
until out=$(bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels push -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name> 2>&1); echo "$(date +%H:%M) $out" | tail -1; echo "$out" | grep -q "successfully pushed"; do sleep 90; done; bash jobs/wait.sh <user>/<project>-<job name> <job name>
```

### `jobs/wait.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Follow a Kaggle kernel until it stops. Write each status change into JOBS.md.
# Usage: bash wait.sh <owner/kernel-slug> "<job name in the JOBS.md row>"
DIR="$(dirname "$0")"
last=""
while true; do
  raw=$(bash "$DIR/kaggle.sh" kernels status "$1" 2>&1)
  case "$raw" in
    *QUEUED*) status="queued" ;;
    *RUNNING*) status="running" ;;
    *COMPLETE*) status="complete" ;;
    *ERROR*) status="failed" ;;
    *CANCEL*) status="cancelled" ;;
    *) status="$last" ;;
  esac
  if [ -n "$status" ] && [ "$status" != "$last" ]; then
    sed -i "/^| [0-9-]* | $2 |/ s/| [a-z ]* |\$/| $status |/" "$DIR/JOBS.md"
    echo "$(date +%H:%M) $status"
    last="$status"
  fi
  case "$status" in complete|failed|cancelled) echo "$raw"; exit 0 ;; esac
  sleep 60
done
```

`wait.sh` calls `kaggle.sh`. Thus it uses the same account as the push.

The job folder `jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>/` has the kernel `<user>/<project>-<job name>` and the row `<job name>` in `JOBS.md`. The call:

```bash
# From the project folder, after the push of the kernel:
bash jobs/wait.sh <user>/<project>-<job name> <job name>
```

Output: one line for each status change. The last line is the final status from Kaggle.

```
13:48 running
18:52 complete
<user>/<project>-<job name> has status "KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE"
```

Run it as a background task, because it waits until the kernel stops (minutes or hours).

### Rules for the follow-up

- Start `wait.sh` after each push: for a new job and also for a new version of an old job. Without it, the status in `JOBS.md` stays old.
- Use one background task for each job. A tool that waits for a background task gives a notice only when the complete task stops. If one task follows two jobs, the end of the first job stays without a notice until the second job ends.
- If a `wait.sh` process stops (for example after a move of the folder), start it again.
- When a job ends, check that its row shows the final status.

## 7. Protect long runs

- **Smoke test.** Before a run of many hours, run the same code path on a small part of the data. Use a CPU kernel, or the local machine if it has enough memory. The test must do all steps, also the final steps (selection, reports, final files). An error at the end of a long run loses all its results.
- **Early checks.** Put cheap checks at the start. If a check fails, stop the job. Example: after a small part of a data generation, compare a statistic of the new data with the expected value. If it is wrong, the job stops before the long part.
- **Deadline.** A long loop gets a deadline (for example 9 hours). After it, no new batch starts, and the job writes its results before the 12-hour limit.
- **No heavy work on the local machine.** The local machine does only small checks. It can stop a process if the memory is low.

## 8. Outputs

1. List the files and their sizes: `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels files <user>/<project>-<job name>`.
2. Download only the small files into the output folder of the job:

   ```bash
   bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels output <user>/<project>-<job name> -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>/output --file-pattern '(json|csv|png)$'
   ```

   The pattern is a regular expression for the complete path. Do not start it with `^`.
3. Delete the downloaded `.log` file if it is not necessary.
4. Commit the small results.

Write large intermediate data only to `/kaggle/temp/` or to `/kaggle/working/cache/`. Write small results as CSV or JSON.

## 9. Records

### `jobs/JOBS.md`

The file starts with a short procedure (sections 6 and 8), then the table:

```markdown
Status values: to run, waiting for another job, queued, running, complete, failed, cancelled. The status cell has only one of these values, because `wait.sh` changes it. Put results into the comment.

| Date | Job | Folder | Link | Comment | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| YYYY-MM-DD | <job name> | `YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>` | [<project>-<job name>](https://www.kaggle.com/code/<user>/<project>-<job name>) | <what the job does; the main results after the end> | complete |
```

- The column Job is the name that `wait.sh` gets as its second argument.
- The status cell has one word only. A result in this cell stops `wait.sh`, because its pattern does not match.
- One job folder has one row. A new version of the job (for example after an error) uses the same row and gets a note in the comment, for example "Version 1: out of memory on GPU 0".
- A second row of the same job causes errors: `wait.sh` changes all rows with the job name.

### A table of results (optional)

Some projects need a table that compares the methods. The columns depend on the project, so decide them at the start of the project. If the project has such a table, these rules help:

- Each row has t

26	## X2
27	
28	### Explanations of what no one can hear: how much of an audio model's decision, and of its explanation, lies below the masking threshold
29	
30	Every bin of a spectrogram is either audible or masked by louder neighbours, and the masking threshold from psychoacoustics (the model inside MP3) says which. Deleting all energy below the threshold is a change no listener can hear. You will build the threshold, delete the sub-threshold energy, and measure per model how much of the decision and how much of the attribution mass disappears, across five tasks and three architectures. Then you will test whether that number predicts a model's accuracy drop under codecs, which discard the same energy first, and audit listenable explanations for the share of their audio that nobody can hear.
31	
32	measurement
33	course form: own experiment, with a new metric and a software package
34	compute: one workstation GPU
35	
36	#### The question
37	
38	How much of what audio models compute rests on inaudible energy, how much of their explanations points at it, and does inaudible reliance predict a model's robustness to codecs?
39	
40	#### What is known
41	
42	Psychoacoustic attacks on speech recognition (2018, 2019) hide perturbations under the masking threshold and succeed, which shows that models respond to energy listeners cannot hear. A 2026 causal analysis finds that a practically inaudible change to one frequency flips an audio classifier's decision in over half the cases. Codec robustness of deepfake detectors (2025) and of provenance attribution (2026) was measured without its cause. Listenable explanations (2022, 2024) return audio the user is meant to hear, with no check that it is audible. A 2026 preprint moves the attribution maps of deepfake detectors with inaudible perturbations. Nobody has measured inaudible reliance as a property of models and of explanations, or linked it to codec robustness.
43	
44	#### Terms used
45	
46	masking threshold
47	: the level, per time-frequency bin, below which a listener cannot hear energy because louder neighbouring sound masks it. Computed by a psychoacoustic model from the signal itself.
48	
49	sub-threshold deletion
50	: removing every bin below the threshold and resynthesizing the waveform. By construction the listener hears no change.
51	
52	inaudible reliance
53	: the change in a model's output under sub-threshold deletion, and the share of an attribution map's mass in sub-threshold bins.
54	
55	#### First steps
56	
57	- Implement the masking threshold (the MPEG psychoacoustic model, or an open implementation you have checked) and confirm on ten clips, by listening, that the sub-threshold deletion is inaudible to the team.
58	- Run one classifier on 100 clips before and after the deletion and report the output change against the change between two different clips.
59	- Write down the refuting result.
60	
61	#### Plan
62	
63	- Set up five tasks with public models and data: speech recognition (Whisper), speaker verification, sound tagging (the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs), bird sound classification (BirdNET), and deepfake detection (AASIST, a SONICS detector). Use three architectures where the task has them and 300 clips per task.
64	- Measure the decision change under sub-threshold deletion per model and task, with the between-clip control and bootstrap intervals, at two stated playback levels and with two masking models.
65	- Measure the inaudible mass of four attribution methods (Integrated Gradients, Grad-CAM, LRP, occlusion) on the common grid, with a random-map control.
66	- Measure each model's accuracy drop under MP3 and Opus at three bitrates and test whether inaudible reliance predicts it across models.
67	- Audit listenable maps: the share of a listenable explanation's energy below the threshold of the mix it is played in. Build an audible-by-construction variant (masks restricted to audible bins) and report its faithfulness cost.
68	- Release the threshold code, the deletion, the metric and the tables as a package.
69	
70	#### What you deliver
71	
72	You deliver an inaudible-reliance number for about fifteen model-and-task pairs and an inaudible-mass number for every explainer on them, the codec-prediction table, the audibility audit of listenable maps with the audible variant, and a package that computes the metric on any model. If the numbers are near zero everywhere, you have shown that these models hear what listeners hear, and the metric becomes a certificate worth reporting.
73	
74	#### What would refute it
75	
76	The decision change and the attribution mass below threshold stay within the between-clip control for every model and task, at both playback levels and under both masking models.
77	
78	#### Where the paper could go
79	
80	Interspeech. ICASSP. WASPAA. A machine learning venue if the codec prediction holds.
81	
82	#### What you need
83	
84	Whisper, a speaker verifier, the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs, BirdNET, AASIST, a SONICS detector. LibriSpeech, a VoxCeleb test set, ESC-50 or an AudioSet evaluation subset, a bird sound set, ASVspoof 2019, SONICS. An MP3 and Opus encoder. Captum, Zennit. The listenable-maps code. One GPU, inference only.
85	
86	#### Compute
87	
88	one workstation GPU
89	
90	#### Watch out for
91	
92	A masking model is an approximation and depends on the playback level. State the level, use two masking models and report both. Resynthesis after deletion can add artifacts of its own. Check the deletion by ear on a sample of every task and keep the phase. The bird sound set's licence must allow research use.
93	
94	#### Read first
95	
96	- Adversarial Attacks Against Automatic Speech Recognition Systems via Psychoacoustic Hiding ([arXiv:1808.05665](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05665))
97	- Imperceptible, Robust, and Targeted Adversarial Examples for Automatic Speech Recognition ([arXiv:1903.10346](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10346))
98	- I Guess That's Why They Call it the Blues: Causal Analysis for Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2601.16675](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16675))
99	- Measuring the Robustness of Audio Deepfake Detection under Real-World Corruptions ([arXiv:2503.17577](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17577))
100	- Clean Accuracy Does Not Guarantee Provenance Robustness: A Prospective Codec-Stress Evaluation of Audio Attribution ([arXiv:2609.07981](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07981))
101	- Listen to Interpret: Post-hoc Interpretability for Audio Networks with NMF ([arXiv:2202.11479](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.11479))
102	- Listenable Maps for Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2403.13086](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13086))
103	- Listenable Maps for Zero-Shot Audio Classifiers ([arXiv:2405.17615](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17615))
104	- The Perceived Fragility of Explanations in Audio Models: Manipulation of Attribution with Unchanged Predictions ([arXiv:2606.14466](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14466))
105	- A Framework for Evaluating Faithfulness in Explainable AI for Machine Anomalous Sound Detection ([arXiv:2601.19017](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19017))
106	
107	## Toolbox
108	
109	You can use any tools you like. Say in the paper what you used. Good starting points: Captum and Zennit for attribution, Quantus for metrics, the audioLIME repository for LIME on audio. Compare maps on one common time-frequency grid so that numbers across models mean the same thing. Give every claim a control (a random map, or a random perturbation of the same size) and report bootstrap intervals over clips. Call a difference a difference only when the intervals say so.
110	
111	Datasets you can start from: ASVspoof 2019 and 2021, In-the-Wild, PartialSpoof, SONICS, FakeMusicCaps, LibriSpeech, a VoxCeleb test set, ESC-50, a bird sound set, a public MIDI corpus. Models you can start from: AASIST, RawNet2, a wav2vec 2.0 detector, the SONICS detectors, the Audio Spectrogram Transformer, PANNs, Whisper, BirdNET, the listenable-maps code. Check every licence before you download.
112	# SIWY
113	# Experiments on Kaggle
114	
115	This document describes a method to run experiments with models on Kaggle from a local repository. It is a collection of rules and lessons from real projects. A project can use only the parts that it needs, and change them for its own work.
116	
117	The local machine has the code and the records. Kaggle does the heavy computation. Git connects the two.
118	
119	## 1. Local setup
120	
121	The local machine needs these items:
122	
123	| Item | Where | What to do |
124	|---|---|---|
125	| Kaggle account | kaggle.com | Do the phone verification (Settings). Without it, a kernel gets no GPU and no internet. |
126	| Python environment | `.venv` in the root folder of the repository | Make it with uv (see the README or the instructions of the repository). |
127	| Kaggle CLI | the package `kaggle` in `requirements.txt` | Install it into `.venv`. Version 2.2.5 works. Call it only through `jobs/kaggle.sh`. |
128	| API token | `~/.kaggle/access_token` or `.kaggle/access_token` of the project | On kaggle.com, open Settings, API, and generate a new token. Write the token into the file as one line. |
129	| Access to the data | the private Kaggle dataset of the project | The owner of the dataset shares it with the account. |
130	| Git remote | a public repository with the project branch | The kernels clone the code from it (section 4). |
131	
132	Do these steps:
133	
134	1. Install the environment:
135	
136	   ```bash
137	   uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
138	   uv pip install --python .venv -r requirements.txt
139	   ```
140	
141	2. Write the token into a file (see "Select the Kaggle account").
142	3. Do a test of the connection. The command shows the kernels of the account:
143	
144	   ```bash
145	   bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels list --mine
146	   ```
147	
148	Do not commit the token. It gives full access to the account.
149	
150	### Select the Kaggle account
151	
152	The script `jobs/kaggle.sh` selects the token. Then it runs the Kaggle CLI from `.venv`. People, agents and other scripts use the same command. Nobody sets an environment variable or gives the token in a command.
153	
154	| Token file | Account |
155	|---|---|
156	| `.kaggle/access_token` in the project folder, not empty | The account of the project. Only this project uses it. |
157	| No project token | The personal account of the machine (`~/.kaggle/access_token`). All projects without a project token use it. |
158	
159	The project token has priority. The script gives it to the CLI in the variable `KAGGLE_API_TOKEN`.
160	
161	To use the personal account, do these steps once on each machine:
162	
163	1. Write the token into the file:
164	
165	   ```bash
166	   mkdir -p ~/.kaggle
167	   echo "<token>" > ~/.kaggle/access_token
168	   chmod 600 ~/.kaggle/access_token
169	   ```
170	
171	2. Make sure that the project has no `.kaggle/access_token`, or that the file is empty.
172	
173	To use a different account for one project, do these steps in the project folder:
174	
175	1. Make sure that `.gitignore` has the line `.kaggle/`.
176	2. Write the token of the project account into the file:
177	
178	   ```bash
179	   mkdir -p .kaggle
180	   echo "<token>" > .kaggle/access_token
181	   chmod 600 .kaggle/access_token
182	   ```
183	
184	3. Check the account. The line `username` must show the project account:
185	
186	   ```bash
187	   bash jobs/kaggle.sh config view
188	   ```
189	
190	`.gitignore` prevents an accidental commit of the token. It does not hide the token from a program of the same user.
191	
192	### `jobs/kaggle.sh`
193	
194	```bash
195	#!/usr/bin/env bash
196	# Run the Kaggle CLI of the project with the correct account.
197	# Usage: bash jobs/kaggle.sh <arguments of the kaggle command>
198	# If .kaggle/access_token of the project is not empty, the CLI uses this token.
199	# Otherwise the CLI uses the personal credentials (~/.kaggle/access_token).
200	set -euo pipefail
201	ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
202	TOKEN="$ROOT/.kaggle/access_token"
203	# The value, not the path: a Windows Python does not know the Git Bash paths.
204	if [ -s "$TOKEN" ]; then
205	  export KAGGLE_API_TOKEN="$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$TOKEN")"
206	fi
207	for KAGGLE in "$ROOT/.venv/Scripts/kaggle.exe" "$ROOT/.venv/bin/kaggle"; do
208	  [ -x "$KAGGLE" ] && exec "$KAGGLE" "$@"
209	done
210	echo "kaggle.sh: no Kaggle CLI in $ROOT/.venv" >&2
211	exit 127
212	```
213	
214	The script looks for `.kaggle/` and `.venv/` in the folder above `jobs/`. Change `ROOT` for a different structure. The examples in this document call the script from the project folder.
215	
216	## 2. Platform facts
217	
218	| Item | Value |
219	|---|---|
220	| GPU machine | `"machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4"` gives 2x Tesla T4, 15 GB of memory each. |
221	| GPU sessions at the same time | 2 for each account. A third push fails with "Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached". |
222	| GPU time | A weekly quota (approximately 30 hours). A session counts its hours, not the number of its GPUs. |
223	| CPU sessions | 4 cores and approximately 30 GB of RAM. They do not use the GPU quota. |
224	| Session limit | 12 hours. |
225	| Output folder | `/kaggle/working/`, approximately 20 GB. Only this folder is kept after the session. |
226	| Temporary folder | `/kaggle/temp/`. It is deleted after the session. |
227	| Input data | `/kaggle/input/<slug>/...`, read-only. |
228	| Python | 3.13 (2026). The local environment can differ. Do not use features of one version only. |
229	| Account | GPU and internet need a phone verification of the account. Without it, a GPU kernel runs on the CPU and no error occurs. |
230	
231	Important behavior:
232	
233	- If a kernel fails (status ERROR), Kaggle deletes its complete output. Hours of results can be lost.
234	- The CLI cannot stop a kernel. Only the web page can cancel it.
235	- The CLI does not give the version ID of a run. Thus use one kernel (notebook) for each job, not many versions of one kernel.
236	- `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels logs -f <user>/<project>-<job name>` shows the live log. The output of child processes is sometimes not in it.
237	- Use `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels status <user>/<project>-<job name>` for the state: QUEUED, RUNNING, COMPLETE, ERROR or CANCEL.
238	
239	## 3. Repository structure
240	
241	```
242	<project>/
243	  src/                    all logic (Python modules)
244	  jobs/
245	    JOBS.md               the list of all jobs and their status
246	    kaggle.sh             runs the Kaggle CLI with the token of the project or the personal token
247	    wait.sh               follows one kernel and writes its status into JOBS.md
248	    runs/
249	      YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job>/  one folder for each job (NN: the number of the job in the project)
250	        run.py              the script that Kaggle runs
251	        kernel-metadata.json
252	        <codename>.yaml     one config for each experiment of the job
253	        output/             the small results, with the same paths as /kaggle/working/
254	          <codename>/       metrics.json, report_*.csv, train_log.csv, ...
255	```
256	
257	### Names
258	
259	The job folder `YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>` identifies a job. NN is the number of the job in the project (01, 02, 03, ...). It does not start again on a new day. Thus the folders sort in the order of the jobs, and the number alone identifies a job. One job folder is one Kaggle kernel and one row in `JOBS.md`.
260	
261	| Name | Where it occurs |
262	|---|---|
263	| Job folder, for example `2026-11-01_16_unet-v7ab` | The folder in `jobs/runs/` and the column Folder in `JOBS.md`. |
264	| Job name: the last part of the job folder, for example `unet-v7ab` | The kernel id (`<user>/<project>-unet-v7ab`), the column Job in `JOBS.md`, the second argument of `wait.sh`. |
265	| Codename, for example `unet-v7a` | The config file (`unet-v7a.yaml`), the output folder (`output/unet-v7a/`), and a table of results, if the project has one. |
266	
267	- Each name is unique in the project. A search for a name finds all files of this job or experiment.
268	- A job has one or more codenames: one config file and one output folder for each codename.
269	- Variants of one idea get letters: `unet-v7a`, `unet-v7b`, `unet-v7c`, `unet-v7d`.
270	- The job name is the common part of its codenames plus their letters. The job `unet-v7ab` runs `unet-v7a` and `unet-v7b`, and the job `unet-v7cd` runs `unet-v7c` and `unet-v7d`.
271	- If a job has only one experiment, its codename is the job name.
272	- Use only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Kaggle makes the kernel slug from the title, and other characters change.
273	
274	### Rules
275	
276	- A job is one Kaggle kernel. A job can run more than one experiment (codename), for example one on each GPU.
277	- The config of an experiment is in the folder of the job that runs it. There is no separate folder for configs.
278	- The folder of a job does not change after the start. A new variant gets a new folder.
279	- The job folders are in `jobs/runs/`. Thus `jobs/` shows only `JOBS.md`, `kaggle.sh`, `wait.sh` and `runs/`, also when there are many jobs.
280	- `output/` keeps only small files. Data, model weights and caches stay on Kaggle.
281	
282	A function finds a config from its codename:
283	
284	```python
285	RUNS_DIR = PROJECT_DIR / "jobs" / "runs"
286	
287	def load_config(codename: str) -> dict:
288	    matches = sorted(RUNS_DIR.glob(f"*/{codename}.yaml"))
289	    if len(matches) != 1:
290	        raise FileNotFoundError(f"need exactly one config for {codename}, found {matches}")
291	    cfg = yaml.safe_load(matches[0].read_text())
292	    cfg["codename"] = codename
293	    return cfg
294	```
295	
296	Lines for `.gitignore`. They keep data, model weights and logs out of git:
297	
298	```
299	**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.npy
300	**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.npz
301	**/jobs/runs/*/output/**/*.log
302	*.pt
303	*.zip
304	```
305	
306	## 4. Code and data on Kaggle
307	
308	### Code
309	
310	The kernel clones the project branch from a public repository. Thus every run uses code from git, and the commit hash goes into the log. Push the code before the push of the kernel.
311	
312	If the repository has more than one project, clone only the project folder with a sparse checkout. The templates below do this. If the project is the complete repository, clone the complete repository and remove the `sparse-checkout` line:
313	
314	```python
315	subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, REPO, CLONE], check=True)
316	sys.path.insert(0, CLONE)
317	```
318	
319	Clone into `/tmp`, not into `/kaggle/working`. Otherwise the clone becomes a part of the output.
320	
321	### Data
322	
323	- Keep the data in a private Kaggle dataset. Upload the original zip as one file, not thousands of small files. Share the dataset with the team.
324	- The output of one kernel can be the input of another kernel: `"kernel_sources": ["<user>/<project>-<job name>"]`. Thus a data set or model weights from one job go to the next job without a download.
325	- The path under `/kaggle/input` can change. Find files with a recursive search, for example `Path("/kaggle/input").rglob("val.npy")`.
326	- To make a dataset from a kernel output, use the page of the kernel: Output, New Dataset. Kaggle extracts a zip to a folder with the name of the zip. If the output also has a folder with this name, the creation fails ("Directory already exists"). Thus give a zip a name like `<codename>-set.zip`.
327	
328	### `kernel-metadata.json`
329	
330	```json
331	{
332	  "id": "<user>/<project>-<job name>",
333	  "title": "<project>-<job name>",
334	  "code_file": "run.py",
335	  "language": "python",
336	  "kernel_type": "script",
337	  "is_private": true,
338	  "enable_gpu": true,
339	  "enable_internet": true,
340	  "machine_shape": "NvidiaTeslaT4",
341	  "dataset_sources": ["<user>/<dataset>"],
342	  "competition_sources": [],
343	  "kernel_sources": []
344	}
345	```
346	
347	For a CPU job, use `"enable_gpu": false` and remove `machine_shape`.
348	
349	The `<user>` in the `id` must be the username of the account that `jobs/kaggle.sh` selects. Otherwise the push and the status fail with "Permission denied".
350	
351	### `run.py` for one experiment on one GPU
352	
353	```python
354	"""<What the job does, in one or two sentences.>"""
355	import subprocess
356	import sys
357	
358	REPO = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>.git"
359	BRANCH = "<project branch>"
360	PROJECT = "<project folder>"
361	CLONE = "/tmp/repo"  # Not in the output folder, so the clone is not an output.
362	CODENAMES = ["<codename>"]
363	
364	import torch
365	
366	# A long job on the CPU wastes hours, so stop immediately without a GPU.
367	assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "no GPU: check the phone verification of the account"
368	
369	subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse", REPO, CLONE], check=True)
370	subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "sparse-checkout", "set", PROJECT], check=True)
371	print("commit", subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "rev-parse", "HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
372	sys.path.insert(0, f"{CLONE}/{PROJECT}")
373	
374	from src.config import load_config
375	from src.experiment import run_experiment
376	
377	for codename in CODENAMES:
378	    run_experiment(load_config(codename))
379	```
380	
381	## 5. Use of the two GPUs
382	
383	A T4 x2 session has two GPUs, and the quota counts the session. A job that uses one GPU wastes half of its cost.
384	
385	One process on each GPU uses both GPUs. Each process does its own work: one experiment, or one half of the data (shard).
386	
387	### `run.py` for two experiments, one on each GPU
388	
389	```python
390	"""Run two experiments at the same time, one on each GPU."""
391	import subprocess
392	import sys
393	
394	REPO = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>.git"
395	BRANCH = "<project branch>"
396	PROJECT = "<project folder>"
397	CLONE = "/tmp/repo"  # Not in the output folder, so the clone is not an output.
398	CODENAMES = ["<codename a>", "<codename b>"]
399	
400	
401	def run(codename: str, gpu: int) -> None:
402	    sys.path.insert(0, f"{CLONE}/{PROJECT}")
403	    from src.config import load_config
404	    from src.experiment import run_experiment
405	    run_experiment(load_config(codename), f"cuda:{gpu}")
406	
407	
408	# A new process imports this file again, so the clone and the start must be only in the main process.
409	if __name__ == "__main__":
410	    import torch
411	
412	    assert torch.cuda.device_count() == 2, "this job needs 2 GPUs (T4 x2)"
413	    subprocess.run(["git", "clone", "--depth", "1", "--branch", BRANCH, "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse", REPO, CLONE], check=True)
414	    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "sparse-checkout", "set", PROJECT], check=True)
415	    print("commit", subprocess.run(["git", "-C", CLONE, "rev-parse", "HEAD"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())
416	    with torch.multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Pool(2) as pool:
417	        pool.starmap(run, [(codename, gpu) for gpu, codename in enumerate(CODENAMES)])
418	```
419	
420	Rules for this pattern:
421	
422	- Use the `spawn` context. CUDA does not work in a process from `fork`.
423	- Put the main code under `if __name__ == "__main__":`. Each new process imports `run.py` again.
424	- The experiment function gets the device as an argument, and it calls `torch.cuda.set_device(device)`.
425	- Each process writes its results into its own folder, `/kaggle/working/<codename>/`.
426	- The main process must not keep GPU memory. If it used the GPU before the start of the pool, call `torch.cuda.empty_cache()`. In one job, the main process kept 12 GB of cache on GPU 0, and the process for GPU 0 failed with "CUDA out of memory".
427	- If one process fails, the complete job fails, and Kaggle deletes the output of both experiments. Thus do a smoke test first (section 7).
428	- Two jobs with two experiments each give four experiments at the same time.
429	- Two processes share the RAM of the session. Each process must stay below approximately half of it.
430	
431	For a CPU job, use `multiprocessing.Pool(4)` for the 4 cores.
432	
433	## 6. Start and follow a job
434	
435	### Start
436	
437	1. Commit and push the code.
438	2. Add a row to `jobs/JOBS.md` with the status `to run`.
439	3. Push the kernel and start `wait.sh` for it.
440	
441	The push sends `run.py` and `kernel-metadata.json` of the job folder to Kaggle and starts the kernel:
442	
443	```bash
444	# From the project folder:
445	bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels push -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>
446	```
447	
448	Output if the push is correct:
449	
450	```
451	Kernel version 1 successfully pushed.  Please check progress at https://www.kaggle.com/code/<user>/<project>-<job name>
452	```
453	
454	The first push makes the kernel. A second push of the same folder makes version 2 of the same kernel.
455	
456	If two GPU sessions are active, the push fails. This loop tries again until a slot is free, and then follows the job:
457	
458	```bash
459	until out=$(bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels push -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name> 2>&1); echo "$(date +%H:%M) $out" | tail -1; echo "$out" | grep -q "successfully pushed"; do sleep 90; done; bash jobs/wait.sh <user>/<project>-<job name> <job name>
460	```
461	
462	### `jobs/wait.sh`
463	
464	```bash
465	#!/usr/bin/env bash
466	# Follow a Kaggle kernel until it stops. Write each status change into JOBS.md.
467	# Usage: bash wait.sh <owner/kernel-slug> "<job name in the JOBS.md row>"
468	DIR="$(dirname "$0")"
469	last=""
470	while true; do
471	  raw=$(bash "$DIR/kaggle.sh" kernels status "$1" 2>&1)
472	  case "$raw" in
473	    *QUEUED*) status="queued" ;;
474	    *RUNNING*) status="running" ;;
475	    *COMPLETE*) status="complete" ;;
476	    *ERROR*) status="failed" ;;
477	    *CANCEL*) status="cancelled" ;;
478	    *) status="$last" ;;
479	  esac
480	  if [ -n "$status" ] && [ "$status" != "$last" ]; then
481	    sed -i "/^| [0-9-]* | $2 |/ s/| [a-z ]* |\$/| $status |/" "$DIR/JOBS.md"
482	    echo "$(date +%H:%M) $status"
483	    last="$status"
484	  fi
485	  case "$status" in complete|failed|cancelled) echo "$raw"; exit 0 ;; esac
486	  sleep 60
487	done
488	```
489	
490	`wait.sh` calls `kaggle.sh`. Thus it uses the same account as the push.
491	
492	The job folder `jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>/` has the kernel `<user>/<project>-<job name>` and the row `<job name>` in `JOBS.md`. The call:
493	
494	```bash
495	# From the project folder, after the push of the kernel:
496	bash jobs/wait.sh <user>/<project>-<job name> <job name>
497	```
498	
499	Output: one line for each status change. The last line is the final status from Kaggle.
500	
501	```
502	13:48 running
503	18:52 complete
504	<user>/<project>-<job name> has status "KernelWorkerStatus.COMPLETE"
505	```
506	
507	Run it as a background task, because it waits until the kernel stops (minutes or hours).
508	
509	### Rules for the follow-up
510	
511	- Start `wait.sh` after each push: for a new job and also for a new version of an old job. Without it, the status in `JOBS.md` stays old.
512	- Use one background task for each job. A tool that waits for a background task gives a notice only when the complete task stops. If one task follows two jobs, the end of the first job stays without a notice until the second job ends.
513	- If a `wait.sh` process stops (for example after a move of the folder), start it again.
514	- When a job ends, check that its row shows the final status.
515	
516	## 7. Protect long runs
517	
518	- **Smoke test.** Before a run of many hours, run the same code path on a small part of the data. Use a CPU kernel, or the local machine if it has enough memory. The test must do all steps, also the final steps (selection, reports, final files). An error at the end of a long run loses all its results.
519	- **Early checks.** Put cheap checks at the start. If a check fails, stop the job. Example: after a small part of a data generation, compare a statistic of the new data with the expected value. If it is wrong, the job stops before the long part.
520	- **Deadline.** A long loop gets a deadline (for example 9 hours). After it, no new batch starts, and the job writes its results before the 12-hour limit.
521	- **No heavy work on the local machine.** The local machine does only small checks. It can stop a process if the memory is low.
522	
523	## 8. Outputs
524	
525	1. List the files and their sizes: `bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels files <user>/<project>-<job name>`.
526	2. Download only the small files into the output folder of the job:
527	
528	   ```bash
529	   bash jobs/kaggle.sh kernels output <user>/<project>-<job name> -p jobs/runs/YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>/output --file-pattern '(json|csv|png)$'
530	   ```
531	
532	   The pattern is a regular expression for the complete path. Do not start it with `^`.
533	3. Delete the downloaded `.log` file if it is not necessary.
534	4. Commit the small results.
535	
536	Write large intermediate data only to `/kaggle/temp/` or to `/kaggle/working/cache/`. Write small results as CSV or JSON.
537	
538	## 9. Records
539	
540	### `jobs/JOBS.md`
541	
542	The file starts with a short procedure (sections 6 and 8), then the table:
543	
544	```markdown
545	Status values: to run, waiting for another job, queued, running, complete, failed, cancelled. The status cell has only one of these values, because `wait.sh` changes it. Put results into the comment.
546	
547	| Date | Job | Folder | Link | Comment | Status |
548	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
549	| YYYY-MM-DD | <job name> | `YYYY-MM-DD_NN_<job name>` | [<project>-<job name>](https://www.kaggle.com/code/<user>/<project>-<job name>) | <what the job does; the main results after the end> | complete |
550	```
551	
552	- The column Job is the name that `wait.sh` gets as its second argument.
553	- The status cell has one word only. A result in this cell stops `wait.sh`, because its pattern does not match.
554	- One job folder has one row. A new version of the job (for example after an error) uses the same row and gets a note in the comment, for example "Version 1: out of memory on GPU 0".
555	- A second row of the same job causes errors: `wait.sh` changes all rows with the job name.
556	
557	### A table of results (optional)
558	
559	Some projects need a table that compares the methods. The columns depend on the project, so decide them at the start of the project. If the project has such a table, these rules help:
560	
561	- Each row has the codename and the job folder. Then the config and the results of a row are easy to find.
562	- Write a row as soon as its results are available. Write "pending" only for a value that does not exist yet.
563	- Text above the table tells what each column measures.
564	
565	## 10. Experiment method
566	
567	- **Codenames.** Each experiment has a codename with a version, for example `unet-v7a`. Variants of one idea get letters (section 3).
568	- **One change for each variant.** A group of variants has a common base, and each variant changes one thing. Then the difference shows the effect of this change.
569	- **Split.** Keep a fixed validation split in a file. Keep a small tune part of the train data for thresholds and for the selection of the checkpoint. Use the validation set only for decisions.
570	- **Checkpoints.** Train longer and keep checkpoints (for example after each 5 epochs, in CPU memory). At the end, score each checkpoint with the real metric on the tune part, and keep the best. The loss does not always follow the metric.
571	- **Noise.** Two runs with the same settings and a different seed show the random difference. A difference smaller than this is not a result. Keep a separate `train_seed` if the main seed also selects the data split.

573	origin	https://github.com/FilipLangiewicz/InaudibleXAI.git (push)
